newsitem.title: USA: Waigel sees German growth, opposes IMF gold sales.
newsitem.headline: Waigel sees German growth, opposes IMF gold sales.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Saturday that Germany agreed with forecasts for its economic growth made by the International Monetary Fund, but continued to oppose IMF gold sales.

At a briefing ahead of talks with financial officials from the Group of Seven industrialised nations, Waigel said the IMF's German growth forecasts of 1.3 percent for 1996 and 2.4 percent for 1997 were realistic.
"This meets the expectations of the federal government," Waigel said.
Waigel did not expect any criticism of Germany's economic policy at today's meeting of the G7, which groups Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
He also said he did not expect any controversy about Germany's persistent rejection of a plan to sell a small amount of the IMF's gold reserves to fund aid to the world's poorest countries.
Taking the view that all parties were now aware of each other's positions on this, Waigel said, "Germany continues to oppose gold sales. But I do not expect a controversial discussion on this."

IMF gold sales have been proposed by the United States and Britain as a way to fund debt relief for poor nations without draining richer countries' domestic budgets. Germany has spearheaded a small group of nations which oppose the sales.

Waigel rejected the suggestion that German officials' repeated insistence that there was no urgent need to sell gold now as IMF funding for the aid programme was sufficient to last through beyond the year 2000 meant that Germany would drop its opposition to the proposal further down the road.
"We will do all can to prove that (gold sales) will not be needed in 2002 either," Waigel said.

Asked about the general conditions for growth and the current state of the foreign exchange markets, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, also in Washington for international meetings, said exchange rates now better matched fundamentals.
"Exchange rate developments are better now than they were a year ago," he said, adding that they better reflected the fundamentals of individual countries.

He added that a generally better policy mix in individual nations had contributed to this. Efforts to reduce budget deficits in most countries had taken some of the burden off monetary policy, he added.
"There is a greater internal consistency of policy," he said. "This is a key prerequisite for exchange rate stability."
